title: Lessons with Charles Elgar in Chicago and return to New Orleans jazz
summary: In Chicago in 1911 he studies violin with Elgar, goes back to New Orleans at about 14 and sneaks into the district with Willie Jones. Later he studies harmony at the musical college.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, I came back to, I came to Chicago then, in 1911. And then, uh, Mr. Charles-
There weren't any jazz men around Chicago?

No, there weren't any then. They were all playing, they were all playing Scott Joplin Rags then. And, uh, Elger came from, up from New Orleans, and by knowing my mother from New Orleans, she came. And, uh, they said that Charles had started studying violin, but it didn't do no good. Maybe it was the teacher, or maybe it was him. And so, uh, they brought my violin out, and Elger said, my goodness, they said, man, shouldn't have had a full-size violin like that to teach you? He said, so I started taking lessons from Elger. He's vice president of the union now. And so, uh, uh, on the Elger, then I got started. And, uh, then I studied about two years up here, and then this property mess came up. Mother beat it down to New Orleans, started straightening it out. And so, I was up here by myself, living with some friends of ours. So, finally, I went on back to New Orleans. And, uh, that's when I, then I was about 14 then, and that's when I became interested in the jazz. And started sneaking around in the district and around on Canal Street. And, uh, because I realized that when you, you played a melody straight after you played it once, you played it over again, and you were just doing the same thing. Whereas these jazz bands, I don't know, did we call them jazz bands then? No. Anyhow, no. Anyhow, these bands, when they, after they played it over, and they went to like second night, they put a lot of extra notes in it. And I had enough musical sense to know that there was extra notes to be put in there, and they started awful good. So, um, this boy, Willie Jones and I, we sneaked down the district. We had our long pants on and tried to act like we was 21. And we went around and stood around the side of the, it was summertime most of the time down there. And the door was open. You could hear the music. Joe Oliver. I think Joe Oliver was playing with his band. Man, he was playing all this trumpet, and we just stood on the outside enthralled, you know, by...
Was it mainly brass music, or did you hear violin music, too?

Well, there were a few bands like Robichaud and some of them that played violin. But the main thing that caught our fancy that kind of woke us up to music that was more than playing the straight melody was bands in the district. And then this, on Canal Street, small jazz bands in the original Dixieland band, that woke us up. And this Willie, he caught on, he had a faster ear than all of us kids that were studying music. And he could come back the next day and say, they played this, da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. And he'd do that on the violin. He'd show it to us. And that's why, that's how we got our start, playing a few extra notes.
So then you came back to Chicago and went to school.
I went to a musical college, and then I had to really study that. That's when I studied harmony and composition, and they made me take piano.
